extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of narratology, literary analysis, and creative writers studying narrative theory
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for analyzing and constructing narrative space and focalization in fiction: how space is represented, functions in the fabula, how sensory perception and objects shape spatial meaning, and how vision/focalization frames what is presented. Useful for literary analysis and informed creative writing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Space as a narratological concept
rubrics_metrics.description: The concept of space is sandwiched between focalization (the representation of space constitutes a special case) and place (a category of fabula elements); it is an important aspect of visuality in narrative.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat space both as part of discourse/focalization and as a component of the fabula/place; analyse how representations of space mediate between perception and story-world elements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Space Perceived — three primary senses
rubrics_metrics.description: Three senses are especially involved in the perceptual representation of space: sight, hearing, and touch.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sight conveys shapes, colours, sizes and perspective; sounds help locate distance or proximity; touch indicates proximity and material/substance. Smell may contribute to characterization of space; taste is rarely relevant. Use these perceptual channels to explain how characters experience and present space.

rubrics_metrics.name: Frame versus filling relations
rubrics_metrics.description: Two kinds of relations between characters and space: (1) the space in which the character is situated (or not) regarded as the frame, and (2) the way in which that space is filled.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyse whether a space functions primarily as framing (inner/outer opposition, symbolic boundary) or is characterized by the objects/contents that fill it; consider how boundaries are culturally or narratively invested with meaning (e.g., safety vs. confinement).

rubrics_metrics.name: Symbolic function of frames and boundaries
rubrics_metrics.description: The frame (inner/outer space, doors, thresholds) can have a highly symbolic function and narratives can endorse, reject, change, or play on that meaning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify narrative strategies that exploit invasion of space (horror, allegory such as rape as invasion), and how such thematics shift the moral or political valence of the story.

rubrics_metrics.name: Objects as determinants of spatial status
rubrics_metrics.description: Objects in a space determine the filling: their shape, measurements, colours, and configuration determine the spatial effect (a cluttered room seems smaller; sparsely furnished room larger).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examine whether objects are presented in detail or left vague, and how object arrangement (configuration) affects readers’ perception of the space and its relation to character and action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Construction of semantic content of space (determination, repetition, accumulation, transformation)
rubrics_metrics.description: The semantic content of spatial aspects is constructed similarly to character content via determination, repetition, accumulation, transformation, and relations between various spaces.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess how specific versus general characteristics build an image: general categories allow readers to imagine basic space; added specific qualities incrementally determine the space; repetition emphasizes stability or thematic function.

rubrics_metrics.name: Functions of space: frame, thematized, steady vs dynamic
rubrics_metrics.description: Spaces in a story can function as frames (places of action), be entirely in the background, or be thematized as objects of presentation themselves; spaces can function steadily (fixed frame) or dynamically (allow movement).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When space is thematized it becomes an acting place that can subordinate the fabula; distinguish steady/background spaces from dynamic, movement-enabling spaces (paths, journeys, seas) and analyse their narrative effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Movement through space as narrative strategy
rubrics_metrics.description: Movement of characters can be a strategic transition between spaces (often opposites), a vehicle for change/liberation/knowledge, or simply a presentation of space (including circular/aimless movement portraying labyrinth or confinement).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider whether travel is goal-directed or an allegory of narrative travel; note gendered traditions of travel and how postcolonial/epic revivals can repurpose space as a site of memory and belonging.

rubrics_metrics.name: Space as site of memory and cultural/political meaning
rubrics_metrics.description: Space may become a site of memory (e.g., postcolonial attempts to re-occupy space with a fabula that affirms belonging) or an explicit repository of past trauma and acts of remembrance or forgetting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for spatial galleries, museum-like rooms, or named rooms that dramatize poetological or mnemonic projects; analyse inscriptions, rituals, and rules within spaces (e.g., ‘hospital for words’) that link space to collective/personal memory.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relation between space and character (environmental influence)
rubrics_metrics.description: A person’s living space is connected to character, way of life, possibilities, and mood (e.g., impoverished circumstances, high spaces causing exaltation or depression through inaccessibility).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Map how authors use spatial position, dwelling conditions, and surroundings to signal socioeconomic status, psychological state, or to shape plausibility of actions and attitudes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Spatial presentation and narrative rhythm (durativity and interruption)
rubrics_metrics.description: When a space is presented in great detail, the time sequence is interrupted; spatial indications are durative (often iterative) and repeated to emphasize frame stability against transitory events.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use presence/absence and level of spatial detail to explain rhythm and pacing; detailed descriptions can function as events or pauses, altering chronology and reader attention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explicit vs minimal spatial information
rubrics_metrics.description: There are various ways to present information about space: brief indications (minimal locative cues), more specific brief locative cues, full descriptions, or actions performed with the space (e.g., crashing into a tree, locking someone in).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish incidental locative utterances from descriptive passages; analyse how even minimal locative cues invoke prior presentation and reader construction of the space; actions with space often carry stronger narrative significance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distance and perspective in spatial depiction
rubrics_metrics.description: The distance from which space is presented affects the image: far-away presentations give overview without details; nearby presentations give details without overview.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider chosen narrative distance to explain why certain details are foregrounded or omitted and how that shapes the reader’s mental map of the story-world.

rubrics_metrics.name: Topos/locus and stereotypical space-event combinations
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain places are stereotypically linked to certain events (topos): e.g., declarations of love on a balcony, locus amoenus in medieval literature. Expectations may be fulfilled or frustrated by the narrative.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify conventional place-event pairings and examine whether an author conforms to or subverts those conventions to produce irony, novelty, or thematic comment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Perceptual factors undermining objective presentation
rubrics_metrics.description: Perception depends on many factors — position relative to object, light angle, distance, prior knowledge, psychological attitude — so aiming for objectivity in storytelling is pointless; storytelling is inevitably slanted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When analysing claims to objectivity, enumerate perceptual conditions shaping a vision; treat narrated ‘objectivity’ as a rhetorical stance rather than an absence of mediation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of focalization
rubrics_metrics.description: Focalization is the relation between the vision (the focalizer) and what is seen, perceived — the relation between the vision and what is seen; it belongs in the story layer between linguistic text and fabula.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyse focalization as mediation: the focalizer (subject/agent of seeing) and the focalized (object seen) must be studied separately; track chains of perception and who sees whom (narrative of seeing).

rubrics_metrics.name: Focalizer types: internal (CF) and external (EF) and their effects
rubrics_metrics.description: If the focalizer coincides with a character (character-bound focalizer, CF) the reader is inclined to accept that character’s biased vision; an external, non-character-bound focalizer (EF) can appear objective but still carries implicit bias.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Categorize passages as CF or EF; examine how CF produces limitation or sympathy (e.g., Maisie’s limited vision) and how EF manages apparent neutrality; note whether narrator and focalizer are conflated or distinct.

rubrics_metrics.name: Shifts and alternations of focalization
rubrics_metrics.description: Focalization can shift from one character to another while the narrator remains constant (alternation EF↔CF or multiple CFs); some characters may focalize often while others not at all.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mark focalization shifts and quantify who carries focalization weight; use initials or labels for recurring focalizers to keep analysis clear; consider how shifting focalization creates neutrality, multiplicity of perspectives, or emphasis on particular characters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Focalized object and analytic questions
rubrics_metrics.description: Any element (characters, objects, landscapes, events) can be focalized and its presentation carries interpretation. Relevant analytic questions: (1) What does the character focalize: what is it aimed at? (2) How does it do this: with what attitude does it view things? (3) Who focalizes it: whose focalized object is it?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply the three questions systematically to reveal the interpretative slant of presentation, the attitude/affect shaping it, and the identity/social position of the focalizer producing that vision.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stream-of-consciousness and coinciding visions
rubrics_metrics.description: Sometimes the reader is presented with a vision as directly as possible so that narrator and focalizer cannot be isolated (stream of consciousness), yet the speech act of narrating remains distinct from the vision presented.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish first-person contiguous impressions from narrative mediation; even in a stream-of-consciousness passage, maintain analytic separation between narrator’s reporting act and the focalizer’s immediate perceptions.
